study_identification_part.si4_title: Mapping Neurophysiological Subtypes of Major Depressive Disorder Using Normative Models of the Functional Connectome

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To quantitatively uncover heterogeneity of individual functional connectome abnormalities in MDD using normative modeling and identify reproducible neurophysiological MDD subtypes across the lifespan based on individual deviations in functional connectivity strength (FCS), and to evaluate subtype differences in baseline clinical variables and longitudinal treatment predictive capacity.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis:
Answer: Subtype identification: k-means clustering algorithm based on individual FCS deviation patterns, with optimal cluster number determined by 11 of 22 quality indices. Group comparisons: two-sample t tests for between-group differences in mean deviation maps and overall deviation indices (FDR-corrected q<.05); ANCOVA for differences in correlations between HDRS-17 score and onset age between subtypes. Demographic/clinical comparisons: independent t-tests for age and HDRS item scores (Bonferroni corrected); chi-square tests for categorical variables (medicated proportion, first/recurrent episode). Treatment prediction: support vector regression (SVR) with 5-fold cross-validation to predict HDRS score change after 6-month paroxetine treatment from baseline deviation values, separately for each subtype; one-tailed permutation tests for significance. Effect sizes: Cohen's d for continuous variables, Cramer's V for categorical variables, η²p for ANCOVA.
Confidence Rating: High
Negative Answer Category: Not Negative
Reason: The paper provides detailed description of statistical methods for all major analyses including clustering, group comparisons, demographic/clinical associations, and treatment prediction, with appropriate correction for multiple comparisons.
Supporting Text: We used a data-driven k-means clustering algorithm to explore MDD subtypes with different deviation patterns... The between-group differences in the mean deviation map and the overall deviation indices between patients with MDD and HCs were compared using two-sample t tests. The significance level was corrected for multiple comparisons using the false discovery rate (FDR) method... The severe-deviation subtype had more severe symptoms as measured using the suicide item (d=0.19, p=.044), while the moderate-deviation subtype exhibited more severe symptoms as measured by the work and activities (d=0.29, p=.002) and depressed mood (d=.23, p=.016) items... Support vector regression analysis was conducted to examine the predictive ability of baseline deviation values for treatment response in each patient subtype... the baseline individual deviation map could significantly predict HDRS score changes after treatment for the severe-deviation subtype (r=0.47, p=.019, one-tailed permutation test)

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief:
Answer: Two reproducible neurophysiological subtypes of MDD were identified based on functional connectivity deviations: Subtype 1 (37%) showed severe deviations with hyperconnectivity in DMN/limbic/subcortical areas and hypoconnectivity in sensorimotor/attention areas, while Subtype 2 (63%) showed moderate but opposite deviations; subtypes differed in depressive symptom profiles and treatment prediction ability.
Confidence Rating: High
Negative Answer Category: Not Negative
Reason: The main findings are clearly summarized in the abstract and discussion.
Supporting Text: Our findings indicated great intersubject heterogeneity in the spatial distribution and severity of functional connectome deviations among patients with MDD, which inspired the identification of 2 reproducible neurophysiological subtypes. Subtype 1 showed severe deviations, with positive deviations in the default mode, limbic, and subcortical areas and negative deviations in the sensorimotor and attention areas. Subtype 2 showed a moderate but converse deviation pattern. More importantly, subtype differences were observed in depressive item scores and the predictive ability of baseline deviations for antidepressant treatment outcomes

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed:
Answer: The study identified substantial heterogeneity in functional connectivity strength (FCS) deviations among MDD patients: 72.82% (n=836) showed extreme deviations in at least one region, but spatial overlap was low (<5.88% per region). Two subtypes emerged from k-means clustering (validated by 11/22 quality indices): Subtype 1 (37%, n=425) had severe deviations (positive in DMN/LIM/SUB, negative in sensorimotor/attention areas; absolute d=0.32-1.65), while Subtype 2 (63%, n=723) showed moderate opposite deviations. Subtype 1 patients were older (d=0.16, p=.008), more likely medicated (Cramer's V=0.08, p=.013), scored higher on HDRS suicide item (d=0.19, p=.044), and showed negative correlation between HDRS-17 and onset age (r=-0.24, p=.004); Subtype 2 scored higher on work/activities (d=0.29, p=.002) and depressed mood items (d=0.23, p=.016). Among treatment responders (n=43), baseline deviation patterns predicted 6-month HDRS change only in Subtype 1 (r=0.47, p=.019), with contributions from DMN (24.1%), frontoparietal (16.1%), and ventral attention networks (15.6%). Intersite reproducibility was high (leave-one-site-out overlap >92%; no significant site differences in subtype distribution, χ²₉=14.74, p=.098).

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes:
Answer: The study demonstrates the value of normative modeling for quantifying individual-level heterogeneity in functional connectomes and identifying data-driven neurophysiological subtypes in MDD. Key innovations include: (1) using lifespan normative trajectories rather than simple case-control comparisons to identify individual deviations; (2) achieving high intersite reproducibility through leave-one-site-out validation (overlap >92%); (3) linking neurobiological subtypes to specific clinical profiles (suicide risk vs. anhedonia/depressed mood) and differential treatment prediction capacity. The severe-deviation subtype's positive deviations in DMN/limbic/subcortical regions associated with higher suicide scores and predictable treatment response, while the moderate-deviation subtype's reduced connectivity in these regions linked to core depressive symptoms (anhedonia, mood) but no treatment prediction. This framework may inform future personalized treatment allocation by identifying patients with marked brain alterations who are more likely to benefit from specific interventions.
Confidence Rating: High
Negative Answer Category: Not Negative
Reason: The paper discusses clinical implications and novel methodological contributions throughout the discussion and conclusion.
Supporting Text: These findings shed light on our understanding of different neurobiological mechanisms underlying the clinical heterogeneity of MDD and are essential for developing personalized treatments for this disorder... Unlike the traditional case-control analysis, which provides information only on group-level abnormalities, the normative model considers intersubject differences within the patient and control groups and allows for measuring individual deviations from a typical trajectory

caa10_key_limitations.answer:
Answer: (1) Cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation and trajectory characterization; age effects on subtypes need consideration; (2) Only HDRS-17 item scores available for symptom comparison; cognitive impairments not assessed; (3) Treatment outcome sample was small (n=43) and included only responders (non-responders discontinued or changed treatment), limiting prediction model for treatment-resistant depression; (4) Effect sizes of subtype differences were relatively small, suggesting potential remaining heterogeneity within subtypes; (5) Data collected only in China, may be more representative of Asian population; external validation in other populations needed; (6) Genetic and environmental factors (childhood adversity, life stress) not examined as potential contributors to subtype differences.
Confidence Rating: High
Negative Answer Category: Not Negative
Reason: The paper provides a comprehensive discussion of limitations in a dedicated section.
Supporting Text: Several issues with the current study need to be addressed further. First, our analysis was performed based on data from a cross-sectional sample... Second, in this study, we compared the subtype differences in clinical symptoms using HDRS-17 item scores. The patients with MDD also had varied cognitive impairments, which were not assessed... Third, all the patients who were included in the analysis to predict treatment outcomes were responders... Fourth, although the significance level of our results was corrected for multiple comparisons using the FDR method, the effect sizes of subtype differences are relatively small... Fifth, an episode of MDD may be caused by numerous different factors, such as genetic liability, childhood adversity, and life stress... Finally, we used 10-fold and leave-one-site-out cross-validation... external validation in independent datasets from other populations and demographic groups is needed

- general_notes.Answer: "This is the largest multisite analysis to date (N=2227) for neurophysiological MDD subtyping using normative models. The DIDA-MDD consortium includes two separate datasets from Guangzhou University of Chinese Medicine (GCMU1 and GCMU2) collected on the same scanner but with different scan parameters. Duration of illness mean 2.10±3.60 years; 512 first episode, 79 recurrent episode (many sites NR); 277 medicated, 622 unmedicated; mean HDRS-17 score 21.94±6.47; mean age at illness onset 32.74±12.37 years; mean framewise displacement (FD) was comparable between patients (0.125±0.067 mm) and HCs (0.123±0.063 mm, p=.387). The normative model approach revealed that although most patients (72.82%) showed extreme deviations in at least one region, the specific deviated regions varied greatly across individuals (spatial overlap <6% per region), explaining inconsistencies in prior case-control studies. The study extends previous findings that DMN functional connectivity patterns are important biomarkers for MDD subtyping, now validated in a large Asian population with robust site-effect handling. Previous version published as preprint on bioRxiv: https://doi.org/10.1101/2023.02.13.528399. Validation analyses tested robustness across different FCS thresholds (r=0.15, 0.25), extreme deviation thresholds, and age/sex subgroup models, with overlap rates 92.84%-99.22% compared to main results."
